title: 2 Samuel 4:1–8
context: When Saul’s son Ishbosheth hears that Abner is dead, he loses heart and all Israel is troubled. Two of his captains, Baanah and Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite from Benjamin, are introduced, with a brief note about Beeroth and the Beerothites who fled to Gittaim. The narrator also mentions Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, who became lame at five when his nurse fled with him at the news of Saul and Jonathan’s death. Rechab and Baanah then enter Ishbosheth’s house at midday while he rests, kill and behead him, travel all night by the Arabah, and bring his head to David in Hebron, claiming the LORD has avenged the king. Both traditions read this as a grim account of treachery that hastens the end of Saul’s house, told without excusing the killers.

verses.text: When Saul’s son heard that Abner was dead in Hebron, his hands became feeble, and all the Israelites were troubled.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the news of Abner’s death leaves Ishbosheth weak and all Israel troubled. The king’s response shows how much he depended on Abner, and the people’s alarm shows how unstable the northern kingdom has become without its real leader.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Ishbosheth is not even named in this verse but simply called Saul’s son, which may emphasize his weakness and dependence. Both traditions agree that the collapse of Saul’s house is now accelerating, as the narrative moves toward David’s rule over all Israel.

verses.text: Saul’s son had two men who were captains of raiding bands. The name of one was Baanah and the name of the other Rechab, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin (for Beeroth also is considered a part of Benjamin;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Baanah and Rechab are captains of raiding bands under Ishbosheth, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite from Benjamin. They are men of Saul’s own tribe and in his son’s service, which makes their later betrayal all the more striking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the killers are introduced as trusted men within Ishbosheth’s own circle. Both traditions agree that the narrator is preparing readers for treachery from within, which marks the final unraveling of Saul’s house.

verses.text: and the Beerothites fled to Gittaim, and have lived as foreigners there until today).
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the narrator explains that Beeroth was considered part of Benjamin and that the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and lived there as foreigners. The reason for this flight is not given, and its connection to the rest of the story is uncertain, though some suggest it relates to Saul’s treatment of the Gibeonite cities (compare Joshua 9:17; 2 Samuel 21:1–2).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the uncertainty about why the Beerothites fled and where Gittaim was. Both traditions agree that the aside identifies the killers’ background without explaining their motive, and that readers should be cautious about building interpretations on details the text leaves unexplained.

verses.text: Now Jonathan, Saul’s son, had a son who was lame in his feet. He was five years old when the news came about Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel; and his nurse picked him up and fled. As she hurried to flee, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that the narrator pauses to introduce Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, lamed at five when his nurse fled with him. The aside may signal that with Ishbosheth about to die, Saul’s line will continue only through a disabled child, though the narrator does not state this purpose directly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Mephibosheth will later receive kindness from David for Jonathan’s sake (2 Samuel 9). Both traditions agree that the brief mention prepares for that later story, and both note that the narrator’s exact reason for placing the aside here is not spelled out and is best held tentatively.

verses.text: The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, went out and came at about the heat of the day to the house of Ishbosheth as he took his rest at noon.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Rechab and Baanah come to Ishbosheth’s house in the heat of the day, when he is resting at noon. The detail shows their calculated timing, choosing a moment when the king would be vulnerable, which underlines the deliberate nature of their crime.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe the narrator’s careful attention to the time and setting. Both traditions agree that the account presents the killing as premeditated, and that Ishbosheth’s helplessness at rest makes the act all the more treacherous.

verses.text: They came there into the middle of the house as though they would have fetched wheat, and they struck him in the body; and Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that the killers enter as though to fetch wheat and strike Ishbosheth in the body, then escape. Their pretense of ordinary business recalls Joab’s pretense of a quiet conversation with Abner, linking the two killings as acts of deception.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the parallel with Joab striking Abner in the body (2 Samuel 3:27). Both traditions agree that the narrator draws these two murders together, showing a pattern of treachery that David will have to confront if his kingdom is to be established in justice.

verses.text: Now when they came into the house as he lay on his bed in his bedroom, they struck him, killed him, beheaded him, and took his head, and went by the way of the Arabah all night.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the verse repeats and expands the account: Ishbosheth is killed on his bed in his bedroom, beheaded, and his head carried off by way of the Arabah through the night. The vivid detail emphasizes the brutality and premeditation of the killers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the narrator’s sober and detailed retelling, which leaves no doubt about the nature of the act. Both traditions agree that the killing of a man in his own bed is presented as especially wicked, a point David will make explicitly in verse 11.

verses.text: They brought the head of Ishbosheth to David to Hebron, and said to the king, “Behold, the head of Ishbosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life! The LORD has avenged my lord the king today of Saul and of his offspring.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Rechab and Baanah bring the head to David, claiming the LORD has avenged him of Saul and his offspring. They invoke God’s name to justify their crime, presenting murder as divine vengeance in the hope of reward, which is a serious misuse of the LORD’s name.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the killers assume David will welcome Ishbosheth’s death as serving his interests. Both traditions agree that the claim that the LORD has avenged David is a self-serving interpretation, and both see that God’s purpose for David does not need or approve such crimes.
